concept.name: Information asymmetry
concept.definition: The condition in which some market participants possess payoff-relevant information that others lack. It is the foundational friction of market microstructure theory - in Kyle (1985) prices respond to the net order flow of an informed trader, and in Glosten and Milgrom (1985) the bid-ask spread exists because the specialist cannot distinguish informed from uninformed traders.
concept.intuition: When a dealer cannot tell whether the counterparty knows something, every trade is partly a gamble - so the dealer charges everyone a premium upfront.
concept.mechanics: Informed order flow correlates with future prices, so liquidity providers set quotes to break even against a mixture of informed and uninformed flow and revise quotes as trades reveal information; the spread and price impact are the equilibrium prices of this asymmetry.
concept.failure_modes: Information asymmetry cannot be observed directly, so empirical proxies (PIN-type estimates, spread decompositions) are model-dependent and can disagree; it also varies sharply around news events, defeating static estimates.
concept.misconceptions: Information asymmetry is not limited to illegal insider trading; superior analysis, faster data, or knowledge of one's own large parent order all create it.
concept.example: A trader who knows an earnings surprise is imminent sells aggressively; market makers lose on those sales and recoup the loss by quoting wider spreads to all traders.

citations.source: Kyle, 'Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading', Econometrica 53(6):1315-1335 (Crossref record DOI 10.2307/1913210)
